s: cannibalism is practiced by Polypheme the Cyclops (through the eating of human flesh)
q: but ’tis long Since human flesh I tasted.

s: Silenus tends Cyclops (as a shepherd and household servant)
q: My blooming sons, on yonder distant cliffs, Feed the young lambs; while I at home am stationed The goblet to replenish, and to scrape The rugged floor; to this unholy lord, A minister of impious festivals:

s: Silenus is a father (of the Chorus of Satyrs)
q: SIL. My sons, be silent: bid your followers drive Their flocks into the stony cave.

s: Chorus of Satyrs is a satyrs (the chorus)
q: PERSONS OF THE DRAMA. SILENUS. CHORUS OF SATYRS.

s: Chorus of Satyrs serves Polypheme the Cyclops (as enslaved herdsmen)
q: by one of these Were we made captives, and beneath his roof To slavery are reduced. Our master’s name Is Polypheme; instead of Bacchus’ orgies We tend the flocks of an accursed Cyclops.

s: Ulysses is a king (of Ithaca)
q: ULY. Ulysses, king of Ithaca, and th’ isle Of Cephalenè.

s: Polypheme the Cyclops is a Cyclopes (a Cyclops)
q: O Cyclops, son of Neptune

s: Polypheme the Cyclops is son of Neptune
q: O Cyclops, son of Neptune

s: Polypheme the Cyclops holds Two, the fattest
q: Two, the fattest, Having well viewed and poised them in his hands

s: Polypheme the Cyclops plans to block your passage
q: For in my station rooted, where this cleft Opens a door, will I spread forth my hands And stop your passage!

s: Polypheme the Cyclops has the Cyclops’s eye (one-eyed and capable of sight before the attack)
q: These lids hath Noman Deprived of sight.

s: Polypheme the Cyclops loses the Cyclops’s eye (through the blinding)
q: Ah me! by burning coals I am deprived Of eyesight.

s: Polypheme the Cyclops is blinded by the blinding of Polyphemus (with a burning brand)
q: Ah me! by burning coals I am deprived Of eyesight.

s: Polypheme the Cyclops is predicted by the oracle (to be blinded by Ulysses)
q: Now is that ancient oracle, alas! Accomplished, which foretold, that I by thee, On thy return from Troy, should be deprived Of sight

s: Ulysses commands Grecian companions (during the escape plan)
q: But with me Do thou preserve thyself, for thou art young: And I to Bacchus, to thy ancient friend Far different from this Cyclops, will restore thee.

s: Silenus is a cupbearer (to Polyphemus)
q: What a knave Is this my cupbearer!

s: Silenus is identified with Ganymede (by Polyphemus while intoxicated)
q: I, O Cyclops, Am Jove’s own Ganymede.

s: Bacchus is a god (of wine and pleasure)
q: A god like this to no man will do wrong.

s: Bacchus is the source of wine (Bacchus’s wine) (as a divine power residing wherever it is lodged)
q: In whatsoever place We lodge him, the benignant power resides.

s: Bacchus is associated with the vessel (as a god believed able to dwell in it)
q: But in a bottle how can any god Delight to dwell?

s: Cyclopes are brothers of Polypheme the Cyclops (fellow Cyclopes)
q: This smiling turf Invites me to partake a vernal feast With my Cyclopean brothers.

s: Mount Aetna provides instruments for sacrifice (stems of thorn)
q: Ætna furnished Such instruments for sacrifice, the stems Of thorn.

s: Ilion is destroyed by Ulysses (with consuming flames)
q: It was destined you should suffer A just requital for your impious feast; For I in vain had with consuming flames Laid Ilion waste

s: Ulysses values Grecian companions (as faithful partners of his voyage)
q: True, ’scape I might, already having passed The cavern’s deep recess: but it were mean If I should extricate myself alone, False to the faithful partners of my voyage.

s: Polyphemus’s cave is a rocky cave (inhabited by Polyphemus)
q: Soon as we entered The rocky cave

s: Polyphemus’s cave contains olive pole (ready for use as a weapon)
q: Within the embers near at hand Lies concealed a smoking brand, Torn from its parental tree.

s: wine (Bacchus’s wine) is offered to him
q: having filled a cup With Maron’s juice unmingled, I to him Bore it, that he might drink

s: wine (Bacchus’s wine) is provided by Maron (as unmingled juice)
q: having filled a cup With Maron’s juice unmingled, I to him Bore it, that he might drink

s: olive pole is intended for my purpose
q: this sword shall point An olive pole, which to my purpose suited Lies in the cave: I in the fire will heat

s: the vessel contains wine (Bacchus’s wine) (used as a drinking vessel)
q: Stranger, bring That vessel from the cave.

s: the vessel is kept by Polypheme the Cyclops (for his private drinking)
q: This luscious beverage, must I not impart To cheer my brothers? ULY. Keep it to yourself And you shall seem more honourable.

s: Ulysses plans to blind Polypheme the Cyclops (by driving a heated olive pole into his eye)
q: I in the fire will heat, And, when it flames, direct the hissing brand Full on the Cyclops’ forehead, to extinguish The orb of sight.

s: the voyage home uses the vessel (to carry Ulysses and his companions away)
q: Thee, and thy friends, and thy decrepit sire, This done, aboard my vessel will I place, And from this region with a double tier Of oars convey.

s: the voyage home crosses Sicilia’s waves
q: But to the shore I haste; and to my country Will steer the vessel o’er Sicilia’s waves.

s: Ulysses uses wine (Bacchus’s wine) (to intoxicate Polyphemus)
q: Perceiving he grew merry I plied him with a second cup, well knowing That wine will stagger him: he soon shall feel Such punishment as he deserves.

s: Chorus is a sons of Bacchus
q: Come on, ye sons Of Bacchus, generous youths; for soon dissolved In slumber shall the monster

s: Chorus is deprived of wine (Bacchus’s wine) (for a long time)
q: for we long Have been deprived of the enlivening bowl, Nor entertain a single hope of freedom.

s: Nile waters Egypt
q: Bright are these virgin currents of the Nile Which water Egypt’s soil, and are supplied, Instead of drops from heaven, by molten snow.

s: Proteus has child Theonoe (daughter)
q: A daughter also of majestic mien, Her mother’s darling, in her infant years (Eidothea called by her enraptured sire): But when the blooming maid became mature For nuptial joys, Theonoe was the name They gave her

s: Theoclymenus is son of the deceased
q: the royal son Of the deceased solicits me to wed him

s: Theoclymenus is devoted to gods (dutifully)
q: Called Theoclymenus, because his life Is passed in duteous homage to the gods

s: Theoclymenus is son of the deceased
q: the royal son Of the deceased solicits me to wed him

s: Theoclymenus kills Greek strangers (when they are captured)
q: He slays each Grecian stranger who becomes His captive

s: Theonoe knows All hidden truths
q: Go in, and question The daughter of the Nereid, her who knows All hidden truths, Theonoe

s: Theonoe knows future (through divine privilege)
q: Theonoe was the name They gave her; all the counsels of the gods, The present and the future, well she knew

s: Theonoe is descended from Nereus (maternal grandfather)
q: Such privilege she from her grandsire Nereus Inherited.

s: Helen is daughter of Tyndarus (born in Sparta)
q: But not to fame unknown Are Sparta’s realm, whence I derive my birth, And my sire, Tyndarus.

s: Helen is a wife of Menelaus (in reality)
q: That I again In Sparta, with my husband shall reside, When he discovers that I never went To Troy

s: Pharos is a island (at the mouth of the Nile)
q: SCENE.—PROTEUS’ TOMB, AT THE ENTRANCE OF THEOCLYMENUS’ PALACE IN PHAROS, AN ISLAND AT THE MOUTH OF THE NILE.

s: Helen is protected by Proteus (at his tomb)
q: But honouring my first husband, at this tomb Of Proteus, I a suppliant kneel, to him, To him I sue, to guard my nuptial couch

s: Helen is pursued by Theoclymenus (for marriage)
q: since the darksome grave Hath covered his remains, the royal son Of the deceased solicits me to wed him

s: Helen is reputed to be adulteress (falsely)
q: For ’tis supposed, that treacherous to my lord, I have through Greece blown up the flames of war.

s: the judgment of Paris is a contest over beauty (among Hera, Aphrodite, and Athena)
q: three goddesses, For beauty’s prize contending, in the cave Of Ida, came to Paris; Juno, Venus, And Pallas

s: Paris judges the judgment of Paris (at Ida)
q: Requesting him to end their strife, and judge Whose charms outshone her rivals.

s: Paris takes Helen’s phantom (believing it to be Helen)
q: Paris falsely deemed That he possessed me

s: Juno creates Helen’s phantom (in Helen’s likeness)
q: But Juno, whose defeat Fired with resentment her indignant soul, Our nuptials frustrated; for to the arms Of royal Priam’s son, she gave not me, But in my semblance formed a living image Composed of ether.

s: Hermes takes Helen (through the air)
q: But Mercury, receiving me in folds Of air, and covering with a cloud

s: Proteus rules Pharos (while alive)
q: But Proteus, while he lived, of these domains Was lord, he in the isle of Pharos dwelt,

s: Trojan War lasts ten years (before Troy)
q: There full ten years were spent.

s: Troy has no trace of those proud walls
q: Not a trace Of those proud walls is now to be discerned.

s: the fall and destruction of Troy occurs seven years before the present (nearly)
q: Seven times the fruitful year Hath almost turned around her lingering wheel.

s: storm and dispersal of the Greek fleet disperses Greek fleet (after Troy)
q: Yes; but a storm dispersed their shattered fleet.

s: Leda is a mother of Helen (according to the report)
q: to my mother Leda Jove was borne On rapid wings, the figure of a swan Assuming

s: Leda is dead suicide (by hanging)
q: Around her neck, ’tis said the noble dame Entwined the gliding noose.

s: Proteus rules Egypt (as king)
q: King of all Ægypt; for his wife he gained

s: Ajax is brother of Teucer
q: My brother Ajax, Who died at Troy, was author of my ruin.

s: Ajax dies by suicide (on his own sword)
q: He fell, On his own blade, and perished.

s: Teucer is a son of Telamon (from Salamis)
q: My name is Teucer, Telamon my sire; The land which nurtured me is Salamis.

s: Teucer fights in Trojan War (as a Greek warrior)
q: And having shared in laying waste its bulwarks

s: Teucer seeks Theonoe (to learn his future course)
q: I to these royal mansions came, Wishing to see the prophetess Theonoe

s: Teucer is destined to settle in Salamis (on Cyprus)
q: To Cyprus’ isle, where Phœbus hath foretold That I shall dwell, and on the walls I rear Bestow the name of Salamis

s: Chorus of Grecian dames is a Helen’s attendants (Grecian women)
q: CHORUS OF GRECIAN DAMES (HELEN’S ATTENDANTS).

s: Chorus of Grecian dames serves Helen (as attendants and companions)
q: CHORUS OF GRECIAN DAMES (HELEN’S ATTENDANTS).

s: tomb of Proteus is in Pharos (at the entrance of Theoclymenus’ palace)
q: SCENE.—PROTEUS’ TOMB, AT THE ENTRANCE OF THEOCLYMENUS’ PALACE IN PHAROS

s: Theoclymenus’ palace is in Pharos (at the entrance to Proteus’s tomb)
q: SCENE.—PROTEUS’ TOMB, AT THE ENTRANCE OF THEOCLYMENUS’ PALACE IN PHAROS

s: Proteus is a dead king
q: But Proteus, while he lived, of these domains Was lord

s: Psamathe was wife of Proteus
q: for his wife he gained One of the nymphs who haunt the briny deep, Fair Psamathe

s: Proteus has child Theoclymenus (son)
q: she in the palace bore To him two children, one of them a son Called Theoclymenus

s: Menelaus is stranded in Egypt (after wandering over the sea)
q: This land is Egypt.

s: Helen is a Greek woman (the true Helen)
q: Of Greece: but earnestly I wish to know Whence you derive your origin

s: Helen is daughter of Jove (through divine parentage)
q: Beneath these roofs Jove’s daughter Helen dwells.

s: Helen is wife of Menelaus (her lawful husband)
q: O to thy consort’s arms at length restored!

s: Helen resides in Egypt (after being brought there by divine agency)
q: The son of Jove hath placed me on the banks Of Nile.

s: Helen never visits Troy (only her image is taken there)
q: I never went To that barbarian youth’s adulterous couch By the swift oar impelled

s: Menelaus is son of Atreus
q: Ere thou my father Atreus didst beget, Whose issue by his consort Ærope Were Agamemnon and myself

s: Helen is accused accused (though guiltless)
q: but Tyndarus’ miserable daughter, Though guiltless, hath unjustly been accused.

s: Helen’s phantom is created by Juno (to prevent Paris from obtaining Helen)
q: Lest Paris should obtain me, this exchange Was made by Juno.

s: Helen’s phantom is guarded in cave containing Helen's phantom (by Menelaus’s surviving companions)
q: Within the dark recesses of a cave Having concealed my wife, that guilty cause Of all my woes, and my surviving friends Enjoined to guard her

s: Helen’s phantom vanishes to the skies (in the heavens)
q: Borne to the skies your consort from our sight Hath vanished, in the heavens is she concealed

s: Proteus resides in Egypt
q: Proteus here resides; This land is Egypt.

s: Proteus belongs to This tomb
q: To him belongs This tomb; his son is ruler of this land.

s: Proteus is hostile to the Grecian host (his enmity persists after their arrival)
q: He’s not within; but to the Greeks he bears The greatest enmity.

s: Proteus's son rules Egypt (from Proteus’s palace)
q: To him belongs This tomb; his son is ruler of this land.

s: Menelaus is brother of Agamemnon
q: Whose issue by his consort Ærope Were Agamemnon and myself, two chiefs Of high renown.

s: Proteus's son is a Helen's persecutor (he seeks to force her into marriage)
q: for from the tomb I by this man am dragged, who to the king Will give me, from whose nuptial couch I fled.

s: Theonoe is a prophetic woman (she knows what has happened)
q: By sage Theonoe, who distinctly knows All that hath happened

s: Theonoe foreknows Menelaus's survival (she reports that he is still alive)
q: for she says my lord Is living, and yet views the solar beams

s: Juno creates Helen’s phantom (as a substitute for the true Helen)
q: Lest Paris should obtain me, this exchange Was made by Juno.

s: the Grecian host fight in Trojan War (against Troy)
q: For in thy cause thy lord and his brave troops On Ilion’s coast already have endured Abundant toils.

s: the Grecian host die for Helen’s phantom (believing the phantom to be Helen)
q: for me Beside Scamander’s conscious stream ye died, Through Juno’s arts, because ye falsely deemed Helen by Phrygian Paris was possest

s: Troy is consumed by That dreadful fire
q: That dreadful fire By which the Phrygian bulwarks were consumed Is memorable

s: Egypt contains Theoclymenus’ palace (the palace is the residence of Proteus’s son)
q: But what domain is this, to whom belong These royal mansions? FEMALE SER. Proteus here resides; This land is Egypt.

s: Theoclymenus’ palace belongs to Proteus (the royal mansion of the Egyptian ruler)
q: But what domain is this, to whom belong These royal mansions? FEMALE SER. Proteus here resides

s: Menelaus is husband of Helen (his true consort)
q: You have no wife but me.

s: tomb of Proteus possesses This tomb
q: To him belongs This tomb

s: Fortune is more powerful than nought
q: Nor is it my assertion, but a maxim Among the wise established, that there’s nought More powerful than the dread behests of Fate.

s: prophecy and divination is unreliable false guidance (according to the messenger)
q: But I perceive how vain And how replete with falsehood is the voice Of prophets

s: Menelaus destroys Troy (by war)
q: since I have o’erthrown The battlements of Troy

s: Menelaus suffers from shipwreck of Menelaus (after the fall of Troy)
q: And now a shipwrecked, miserable man, Reft of my friends, I on these shores am cast

s: Menelaus possesses Menelaus's ship (only its keel remains intact)
q: on the keel, The only part which yet remains entire Of all that fabric, scarce could I and Helen, Whom I from Troy have borne, escape with life

s: Helen has betrayed My husband
q: For there is no man who abhors not Helen; ’Tis rumoured through all Greece that I betrayed My husband, and abode beneath the roofs Of wealthy Phrygia.

s: Menelaus survives shipwreck of Menelaus (as the sole reported survivor)
q: Yourself shall be the messenger; relate How you alone escaped his piteous doom, A partner of the voyage with the son Of Atreus, and the witness of his death.

s: Menelaus has wandered for seven years (after the ten years at Troy)
q: MEN. Year after year, besides the ten at Troy, Seven tedious revolutions of the sun.

s: Menelaus possesses the tattered vest (evidence of shipwreck)
q: MEN. This tattered vest will testify my shipwreck.

s: Menelaus possesses the sword (weapon and intended means of resistance)
q: Here stay: for if the king By force should strive to tear you hence, this tomb And your drawn sword will save you

s: Theonoe is a spotless maid (for ever)
q: But now since Juno is disposed To be your friend, with her will I accord: May Venus be propitious, though her rites I never have partaken, and will strive For ever to remain a spotless maid.

s: Theonoe is sibling of Theoclymenus (sister)
q: No: ’tis his sister, her they call Theonoe.

s: Theonoe protects Menelaus (by concealing his arrival)
q: all that you requested me Will I conceal, nor with my counsels aid My brother’s folly;

s: Theonoe protects Helen (by enabling her return to Menelaus)
q: for with injustice should I act If I restored not Helen: had he lived, My sire on thee again would have bestowed Thy consort, and her former lord on Helen.

s: Theoclymenus is a king (ruler of the region)
q: HEL. Lord of this region, royal Proteus’ son.

s: Theoclymenus is a son of Proteus (royal lineage)
q: HEL. Lord of this region, royal Proteus’ son.

s: Juno supports Menelaus (seeking his safe return to Sparta)
q: Juno who was erst thy foe, Now grown benignant, with thy consort safe To Sparta would convey thee,

s: Venus opposes Menelaus (seeking to prevent his return)
q: But Venus wants to frustrate thy return, Lest she should be convicted, or appear At least the palm of beauty to have purchased By vending Helen for a wife to Paris.

s: Venus causes the fictitious nuptials Of Paris (the baleful gift)
q: For there is strife in Heaven; And Jove on thy account this day will hold A council; Juno who was erst thy foe, Now grown benignant, with thy consort safe To Sparta would convey thee, that all Greece May understand that the fictitious nuptials Of Paris, were the baleful gift of Venus.

s: Hermes delivers Helen’s phantom (to Proteus for safekeeping)
q: For Hermes, Commissioned by the blest immortal powers, Hath, at my cost, consigned me to thy sire, To keep me for this husband, who is here And claims me back again:

s: Troy is destroyed by Menelaus (because of Helen’s abduction)
q: And leaving thee, For whom I laid the walls of Ilion waste?

s: the Trojan War lasts for ten years (before Menelaus’ subsequent wanderings)
q: MEN. Year after year, besides the ten at Troy, Seven tedious revolutions of the sun.

s: shipwreck of Menelaus is evidenced by the tattered vest (reported evidence)
q: MEN. This tattered vest will testify my shipwreck.

s: the false funeral plans a vacant tomb (as if you in the sea Had perished)
q: I will allege that ’tis an ancient custom; And of the monarch his permission crave, That I on you, as if you in the sea Had perished, may bestow a vacant tomb.

s: Helen is faithful to Menelaus (through captivity in Egypt)
q: That I have kept Your bed still spotless, may you rest assured.

s: Helen’s escape from Egypt uses the false funeral (to secure a vessel and flee Egypt)
q: I will command a bark to be prepared, From whence into the bosom of the deep Funereal trappings I may cast.

s: fate and the Destinies holds a council (on thy account this day)
q: For there is strife in Heaven; And Jove on thy account this day will hold A council;

s: Justice guides Theonoe (as her governing moral principle)
q: For from my birth, Hath justice in this bosom fixed her shrine:

s: the Chorus supports Justice (affirming the success of an honest cause)
q: CHOR. No impious man e’er prospered: But fairest hopes attend an honest cause.

s: Helen is protected by tomb of Proteus (as a suppliant refuge)
q: Do you see, Close to the tomb, my miserable seat? MEN. I on the ground behold a couch: but what Hast thou to do with that, O wretched woman? HEL. Here I a suppliant bowed, that I might ’scape From those espousals.

s: Helen hinders my bridal rite
q: You hither come an unexpected guest, And are a hindrance to my bridal rite.

s: Helen is represented by Helen’s phantom (the image taken to Troy)
q: Your husband comes, Your Menelaus in this land appears, Reft of his ships, and of your image reft.

s: Menelaus wins renown (at Troy)
q: for the renown I won at Troy, I never will belie, Nor yet returning to the Grecian shore

s: Helen is a daughter of Zeus
q: Thou, Helen, art indeed the child of Jove. The swan, thy sire, inflamed by love, To Leda’s bosom flew:

s: Menelaus is a husband of Helen (first husband)
q: Thee it behoves, O blooming dame, to love Thy present husband, and to lay aside The fond remembrance of thy breathless lord;

s: Menelaus is rescued from the waves (by chance)
q: Some sailors, as he says, By chance passed by, and snatched him from the waves.

s: Menelaus possesses falchion (prepared for battle)
q: But now my lord hath seized A vengeful falchion

s: Menelaus possesses shield (orbed and carried for the escape)
q: With nervous arm he lifts an orbed shield

s: Menelaus possesses spear (carried for the escape)
q: In his right hand protended gleams the spear

s: Theoclymenus is a son of Proteus
q: O Proteus; Theoclymenus thy son Thee, O my father, oft as he goes forth, Oft as he enters these abodes, accosts.

s: Theoclymenus buries Proteus (before my gate)
q: For thee have I interred before my gate, That with thy shade I might hold frequent conference, O Proteus

s: Helen is a wife of Menelaus (first husband)
q: My Menelaus, (Ah, how shall I express myself?) is dead.

s: Theoclymenus provides A swift Phœnician vessel
q: Ye shall have A swift Phœnician vessel.

s: Proteus is a father of Theoclymenus (deceased king)
q: O Proteus; Theoclymenus thy son Thee, O my father, oft as he goes forth, Oft as he enters these abodes, accosts.

s: Proteus has tomb tomb of Proteus (before Theoclymenus’s gate)
q: For thee have I interred before my gate, That with thy shade I might hold frequent conference, O Proteus

s: Theonoe knows Menelaus (knows of his arrival in Egypt)
q: She and this mariner, who when he perished Was present, both concur in the same tale.

s: Theonoe protects Helen (by withholding information from Theoclymenus)
q: For Proteus’ royal daughter, in our schemes Conspiring when her brother questioned her About my lord, no information gave Of his arrival: to my interests true

s: Paris abducts Helen (from hospitable shores to Troy)
q: From hospitable shores, Relying on barbaric oars, The spoiler Paris fled, And o’er the deep to Priam’s realm with pride Bore his imaginary bride

s: Jove is a supreme god (ruler of Heaven)
q: O Jove, thou mighty father, who art called A god supreme in wisdom, from thy heaven Look down, and save us from our woes

s: Jove is father of Helen (in the form of a swan)
q: Thou, Helen, art indeed the child of Jove. The swan, thy sire, inflamed by love, To Leda’s bosom flew:

s: Juno creates Helen’s phantom (to deceive the Greeks)
q: The cloud by Juno formed, beguiled their dazzled sight.

s: Helen’s phantom is a cloud (resembling Helen)
q: Speak you of a cloud, Resembling me? it mounted to the skies.

s: Troy has towers caught fire her towers
q: And flames, as when Jove’s vengeance throws The bolt, have caught her towers and finished Ilion’s woes.

s: the Greeks is transpierced by spears (or crushed beneath the falling ramparts)
q: Unnumbered Greeks, transpierced with spears, Or crushed beneath the falling ramparts, bled

s: Trojans suffer the Trojan War (during the Trojan War)
q: One conference might have closed: now myriads dwell With Pluto in the shades of Hell, And flames, as when Jove’s vengeance throws The bolt, have caught her towers and finished Ilion’s woes.

s: Tyrian bark has capacity fifty oars (provided for the funeral voyage)
q: Go thou, and furnish them a Tyrian bark Of fifty oars, with skilful sailors manned.

s: the funeral rites of Menelaus include empty vest (Greek custom for one lost at sea)
q: To bury in their stead an empty vest.

s: the funeral rites of Menelaus include blood (as the first libation to the dead)
q: Blood is our first libation to the dead.

s: the funeral rites of Menelaus include brazen arms (because Menelaus loved war)
q: Brazen arms: For war was what he loved.

s: Helen’s escape from Egypt uses the funeral rites of Menelaus (as a stratagem)
q: But now my lord hath seized A vengeful falchion, in that mail designed To have been plunged beneath the deep arrayed, With nervous arm he lifts an orbed shield, In his right hand protended gleams the spear, As if with me he was prepared to pay To the deceased due homage.

s: Helen has reputation slandered name (throughout Greece)
q: Yet with imputed crimes malignant fame Through Greece arraigns thy slandered name.

s: false report of Menelaus’s death is reported by Theonoe (to Helen and Theoclymenus)
q: She and this mariner, who when he perished Was present, both concur in the same tale.

s: marriage and fidelity is exemplified by Helen (her continued love for Menelaus)
q: I will; nor shall my husband e’er have cause To blame me

s: Bacchus is honored by Bacchic ritual (through music, dancing, and night-long celebration)
q: And youths, with virgins in a ring, When high from earth with matchless force they spring, Loose streams their hair, they celebrate that god The Bacchanalian votaries own, And waste in dance the sleepless night.

s: Helen remains faithful to Menelaus (despite the reported death of her first husband)
q: Still is he dear, lodged in this faithful breast

s: Helen would inter my departed husband
q: I my departed husband would inter.

s: Helen urges the rites my dearest Menelaus claims (with greater zeal)
q: Hence too with greater zeal will you perform The rites my dearest Menelaus claims, If all due honours you from me receive.

s: Menelaus is a Greek (surviving mariner)
q: He’s a Greek, One of those Greeks who with my husband sailed.

s: Helen is daughter of Jove
q: Jove’s daughter to the shore was borne

s: Helen is named for Athens (an island near it will bear her name)
q: there is an isle Near the Athenian realm, which men shall call Helen in future times, because that spot Received you

s: Menelaus is husband of Helen (her first husband)
q: Sail with your husband, for a prosperous breeze Your voyage shall attend

s: Menelaus is son of Atreus (the son of Atreus)
q: But the son of Atreus, Who had just slain the bull, to his companions Called loudly

s: Menelaus returns to his subject land (Victorious ... from Phrygia’s strand)
q: That Menelaus to his subject land Victorious comes from Phrygia’s strand

s: Menelaus deceives Theoclymenus (by pretending to be dead)
q: Who came in person with a feigned account Of his own death

s: Menelaus resides among the happy islands
q: The wanderer Menelaus shall reside Among the happy islands

s: Theoclymenus is a king (king of Egypt)
q: O thou king Of Ægypt’s realm

s: Theoclymenus rules Egypt (as king)
q: O thou king Of Ægypt’s realm
